analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers to cover at least 48 hours of hospital stay after mastectomy.
analysis.headline: With 224 cosponsors from both parties, the bill never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped health plans from limiting hospital stays after breast cancer surgery to less than 48 hours after a mastectomy or 24 hours after lymph node removal. It also banned insurers from pressuring women to leave early with cash rebates and from penalizing doctors who kept patients longer. A woman and her doctor could still choose an earlier discharge; insurers simply could not force one.
analysis.who_benefits: Women undergoing breast cancer surgery who are covered by group health plans or individual insurance. They would keep the option of at least two nights in the hospital after a mastectomy without needing their insurer's sign-off, and their doctors would be free to keep them longer without losing reimbursement.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Breast cancer surgery patients with insurance

how_it_helps.text: Bars group health plans and insurers from covering less than 48 hours in the hospital after a mastectomy or less than 24 hours after a lymph node dissection, and from requiring preauthorization for that length of stay [S2][S3].
Lets the minimum-stay rule be waived only when the attending doctor decides, in consultation with the patient, that an earlier discharge is appropriate [S3].
Prohibits insurers from denying or dropping a woman's coverage to dodge the rule, offering her money to accept a shorter stay, or cutting a doctor's pay for following it [S3].
Extends the same protections to individually purchased insurance and lets any state law with equal or stronger protections stand in place of the federal rule [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who fund group plans, through the added cost of covering longer hospital stays, which can flow into premiums and plan costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employers with group plans

drawbacks.text: Plans may still apply deductibles and coinsurance to the stay, and the added covered days raise plan costs, which typically show up in higher premiums for everyone enrolled [S3].

A uniform federal minimum can substitute a fixed rule for individualized medical and personal judgment; some patients prefer to recover at home, which the bill accommodates only through the provider-consultation exception [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection targets a documented practice — insurers pushing women out of the hospital within hours of major cancer surgery — and the bill is carefully drafted: a woman and her doctor can still choose an earlier discharge, and plans keep control over deductibles and provider payment rates. The cost is a modest, broad premium increase spread across all insured people, which the bill's supporters judged a fair price for taking the decision away from insurers at the moment of cancer surgery.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees, then to subcommittees, and sat there without a hearing or vote until the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on January 7, 1997, the first day of the 105th Congress [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Commerce Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee, and the Speaker split it between them by jurisdiction [S5].
It was referred to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment on January 22 and the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations on January 31, 1997 [S5].
No further action was recorded; the bill never reached a committee vote or the House floor [S5].
It attracted 224 cosponsors — 201 Democrats, 22 Republicans, and 1 Independent — roughly half the House [S4].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill died with it [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers with group plans, who avoided a mandate to pay for longer hospital stays; no one in Congress was ever recorded voting on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers who avoided the mandate

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 105th Congress and recruited 224 cosponsors for it.

for.name: Rep. John Dingell and the other original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors on the day of introduction, spanning both parties including Republicans Marge Roukema and Jack Quinn.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair Thomas J. Bliley Jr. and the committee to which the bill was first referred
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out; after its January 1997 referral to the Health and Environment Subcommittee, no hearing, markup, or vote was ever recorded.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair William Goodling and the second committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after its referral to the Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee on January 31, 1997.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Insurers writing group and individual coverage
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandated-benefit requirements that would force coverage of longer hospital stays after surgery, a position widely reported during the late-1990s 'drive-through delivery and mastectomy' mandate debates.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 224 cosponsors including 22 Republicans — but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call ever recorded the split.

industries.note: The bill strips insurers of their power to cap hospital stays after breast cancer surgery and to require preauthorization for them, directly cutting a cost-saving tool. Its anti-avoidance provisions also block them from buying women out of the protection.
Guaranteed minimum stays mean more inpatient days billed for mastectomy and lymph node dissection patients. Here the hospitals' interest in longer stays runs with patients' interest in recovery time.
ERISA plans would have to cover the longer stays, raising benefit costs. Their workers and families are the same people the mandate protects, so the cost lands on the side that also benefits.
